extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulemakers, state environmental and utility regulators, and electric cooperative policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Public comments arguing how EPA should design final Section 111(d) emission guidelines, focusing on measurement & verification (EM&V), state plan timelines, flexibility for small utilities, and feasibility of interim and final goals. The page recommends specific procedural and substantive standards EPA should adopt or avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: EM&V methodologies should be as simple as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Given that the cost of EM&V can be a barrier to energy efficiency program adoption, methodologies should be as simple as possible to meet the specific state or program need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor savings upstream of the consumer-utility relationship or at a higher level than some methods used by large IOUs (which can require large sample sizes, rigorous statistical analysis, or in-home visits). Keep methods simple to reduce cost barriers and enable program adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume or mandate existing state EM&V protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should not assume certain state EM&V protocols are the preferred method that other States need to follow and should not limit future EM&V options to the existing energy efficiency paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that existing protocols were designed for kWh-focused programs and may not be appropriate when compliance is based on greenhouse gas emissions levels. Avoid prescribing a single existing protocol as mandatory for all States.

rubrics_metrics.name: States must have flexibility to determine whether/how to implement EE programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Any final rule must provide each State the flexibility to determine whether and how it might implement EE programs to meet its Section 111(d) obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow States to tailor program goals and EM&V approaches to what makes sense for their jurisdiction, including the option not to rely on EE to meet emission targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow unit-by-unit flexibility in adopting EM&V protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Where States adopt EE programs, EPA and the States should allow for unit-by-unit flexibility when adopting EM&V protocols to account for the various utilities, after consideration of their size, resources, and customer base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider differences among utilities (cooperatives vs. large IOUs) and permit tailored EM&V approaches rather than one-size-fits-all methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit use of TRMs, program evaluations, deemed savings, and existing data sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperatives and other organizations implementing EE programs are allowed to follow reliable estimates of energy efficiency savings by using existing technical reference manuals (TRM), program impact evaluation results, and other sources of deemed savings available from larger utilities or state agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage use of available economies-of-scale: TRMs created regionally or by states, evaluations of similar programs, and other deemed-savings sources (provided installation and operation have been verified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow adjustments to deemed savings and require periodic updates
rubrics_metrics.description: Deemed savings may be adjusted to allow for climate or other factors (regional or economic/demographic) that differ from one jurisdiction to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program administrators should base deemed savings on calculations/values derived using UMP protocols when possible, and should update deemed savings periodically to reflect changes in appliance/building codes and new EM&V studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow pooling of EM&V resources and cooperation among utilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Program administrators may consider pooling EM&V resources and jointly conducting evaluations of similar programs through local associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pooling has been used successfully (examples: small utilities in California, Michigan, and the Pacific Northwest). States and small utilities may also coordinate with regional larger utilities or adopt results from evaluations conducted by larger utilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require third-party verification/certification of EE programs
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA and States should not require third party verification or certification of EE programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-party verification can become cost prohibitive and unnecessary because numerous existing mechanisms reflect best practices; compliance requirements alone will ensure programs can be adequately evaluated and verified. Requiring third-party verification would increase costs and time without corresponding benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and accommodate small utilities via a 'small utilities protocol'
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurement protocols should clearly distinguish the unique characteristics and needs of small utilities so they have a reasonable and cost-effective approach for developing EM&V without being required to adopt large-scale EM&V protocols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE's UMP recognized options for small program administrators (deemed savings, use of TRMs, evaluations of similar programs). EPA and States should adopt measures akin to a small utilities protocol because small utilities face higher cost impacts and lower benefits from EE programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base interim and final goals on realistic implementation feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s establishment of stringent interim goals undermines any flexibility for States or utilities to comply with the requirements; interim goal requirements dependent on natural gas use and availability must be based solely on existing infrastructure and cannot be premised on construction of additional capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interim goals should not force reliance on infrastructure (pipelines, transmission lines, nuclear units, or large new renewable build-outs) that cannot be completed within the interim timeline. If goals depend on such infrastructure, EPA must base expectations only on existing capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant States substantially more time to develop and submit SIPs
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should grant States at least five years to submit single-state emission guidelines SIPs, and at least seven years to submit multi-state SIPs; extensions should be liberally granted when a State can demonstrate good faith efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current proposal (~1 year) is impermissibly short given the rule's complexity. Longer time is needed to evaluate compliance approaches, obtain statutory authority, draft plans, and satisfy notice/comment/hearing procedures, especially for multi-state coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend final compliance deadline (recommend at least to 2035)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final compliance deadline must be extended, from 2030 to at least 2035, to account for realistic timeframes States and utilities need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensions account for legislative calendars, time to obtain statutory authority, regulatory rulemakings, and practical implementation (engineering, procurement, construction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explicit time for state legislatures and agencies to act
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should include at least two to three years for state legislatures to act, and allow state regulatory agencies a minimum of 18 months to two years to adopt implementing regulations and draft plans; coordinating regulations among several agencies under a multi-state plan will require additional time (at least two to three years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for varying legislative schedules (annual, biennial) and the need for administrative rulemaking and interagency coordination when setting SIP submission and implementation deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not presume state air agencies can impose measures outside their statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental principle of cooperative Federalism is that state air pollution agencies are not delegates of EPA authority for establishing programs regulating generation, transmission, and use of electricity; measures in the proposal often fall outside their jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must recognize that public utility regulators and possibly legislatures will need to be involved; statutory authority to regulate CO2 and to implement outside-the-fence measures may be lacking and would need to be enacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for long, variable project timelines for infrastructure and generation additions
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects like interstate pipelines, major transmission lines, and new nuclear units take many years (often more than a decade) from planning through operation; the Proposal's interim deadlines do not reflect these realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite examples: Atlantic Coast and Mountain Valley pipelines (multi-year construction), PPL and ITC Midwest transmission projects (years of regulatory delay), V.C. Summer nuclear units and other nuclear projects (10+ years licensing/construction). EPA should not rely on projects that realistically cannot be completed by interim deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that independent power producers and nonregulated suppliers may need inclusion and new authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Many additional sources beyond traditionally regulated electric utility companies would likely be subject to requirements under building blocks 2, 3 and 4; statutory and regulatory means to include these sources must be devised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration of independent power producers and other electricity suppliers (often not regulated by state public utility commissions) into state 111(d) SIPs will require new legislative authority and evaluation of practical and legal issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow liberal SIP extension process based on good faith progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensions should be liberally granted when a State can demonstrate that it is making good faith efforts to develop its plan or when it is working with other States to develop a multi-state or regional plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the proposal, limited extensions are available; NRECA recommends broader flexibility to avoid penalizing states actively engaged in plan development or multi-state cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on Federal Implementation Plans without resolving administrative questions
rubrics_metrics.description: If EPA issues its own plan to a State in lieu of the State’s submittal (a Federal Implementation Plan), significant issues arise as to what entity would administer and implement the plan and whether EPA has resources/authority to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should consider practical administration and implementation responsibilities before resorting to FIPs; the prospect of FIPs raises unresolved operational and statutory concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical Clean Air Act SIP implementation experience to set realistic timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule’s tight implementation deadlines ignore forty-four years of Clean Air Act history where Congress and EPA repeatedly extended timelines for SIP development and attainment due to practical difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize precedents (e.g., 1977 and 1990 Amendments creating multi-year attainment tiers for ozone) showing that complex air quality programs have required multi-year and sometimes multi-decade timeframes; apply similar realism to 111(d) planning and attainment schedules.
